Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The paper investigates quantitative weak mixing of Salem substitutions flows. We prove that for a substitution whose substitution matrix is irreducible over the rationals and the dominant eigenvalue is a Salem number, for almost every suspension flow with a piecewise constant roof function, quantitative weak mixing holds with a rate that is slightly worse than a power of log⁡log\log\log. We do not know if this is sharp, but we do show that for any suspension flow of this kind, quantitative weak mixing with a polynomial rate is impossible. Results for specific systems are often much weaker than for “typical” or “generic” ones. In the Appendix we explain how a minor modification of an argument from Bufetov and Solomyak (2014) yields very weak, but nevertheless quantitative weak mixing estimates of log∗\log^{*} type for the self-similar suspension flow over a Salem substitution. Simultaneously this provides first quantitative decay rates for the Fourier transform of Salem Bernoulli convolutions.

Key words and phrases: 
Substitution dynamical system; Salem numbers; quantitative weak mixing; Bernoulli convolutions
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11K16, 37A30, 37B10, 47A11

1. Introduction

In this paper we study ergodic-theoretic and spectral properties of substitution dynamical systems, more specifically, suspension flows over Salem type substitutions. Substitutions and associated dynamical systems appear in many different contexts, in particular, in the study of interval exchange transformations with a periodic Rauzy induction, translation flows along stable/unstable foliations of pseudo-Anosov diffeormorphisms, see [14]. as well as in mathematics of quasicrystals and “aperiodic order,” see [4].

The basic definitions on substitutions may be found in the standard references [30, 31]. Consider an alphabet with d≥2d\geq 2 symbols, denoted by 𝒜={1,…,d}{\mathcal{A}}=\{1,\dots,d\}. Let 𝒜+{\mathcal{A}}^{+} represent the set of all nonempty words composed of letters from 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. A substitution is a mapping ζ:𝒜→𝒜+\zeta:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{A}}^{+}, which extends naturally to 𝒜+{\mathcal{A}}^{+} and 𝒜ℤ{\mathcal{A}}^{{\mathbb{Z}}} by concatenation. The substitution space consists of all bi-infinite sequences x∈𝒜ℤx\in{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathbb{Z}} such that every word appearing in xx is a subword of ζn​(a)\zeta^{n}(a), for some a∈𝒜a\in{\mathcal{A}} and some n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. The substitution dynamical system is given by the left shift on 𝒜ℤ{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathbb{Z}}, restricted to XζX_{\zeta}, and is denoted by TT.

The substitution matrix 𝖲ζ=(𝖲⁡(i,j)){\sf S}_{\zeta}=({\sf S}(i,j)) is the d×dd\times d matrix where 𝖲⁡(i,j){\sf S}(i,j) represents the number of times the symbol ii appears in ζ⁡(j)\zeta(j). The substitution is called primitive if there exists some n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} such that all entries of 𝖲ζn{\sf S}_{\zeta}^{n} are strictly positive. It is well known that the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action given by the left-shift on a primitive substitution subshift is minimal and uniquely ergodic; see [31]. We assume that the substitution is both primitive and non-periodic, which, in the primitive case, is equivalent to the space XζX_{\zeta} being infinite.

The continuous counterpart comes from considering suspensions over XζX_{\zeta}. Namely, we consider ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-actions obtained as suspension (or special) flows over (Xζ,T)(X_{\zeta},T), with a piecewise-constant roof function depending only on the 1st symbol. Such a function may be identified with a positive suspension vector s→∈ℝ+d\vec{s}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+}, see the next section for details. Substitution ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-actions of this kind appear in the study of translation flows and as tiling dynamical systems on the line. Special choices for the suspension vector are s→=𝟏\vec{s}={\bf 1} (the vector of 11’s), and s→=\vec{s}= the right PF (Perron–Frobenius) eigenvector of 𝖲ζ𝖳{\sf S}_{\zeta}^{\sf T}. With the first choice, we essentially recover the substitution subshift. The second choice is referred to as the self-similar suspension flow.

By a result of Dekking–Keane [15] and Clark–Sadun [13], substitution systems and their suspensions are never strongly mixing, however, they may be weakly mixing, see [19] for an algebraic characterization. Here our focus is on the property of quantitative weak mixing (QWM), which has been intensively studied recently.

Weak mixing is a fundamental property of measure-preserving systems; it has several equivalent characterizations, see, e.g., [16]. One of them is absence of non-trivial discrete spectrum; equivalently, the spectral measure σf\sigma_{f} corresponding to any L2L^{2}-function of mean zero has no point masses. Given a weakly mixing system, it is natural to ask what is the rate of decay of the spectral measure of a small neighborhood of a point, as the radius tends to zero, for a sufficiently “nice” test function ff. Another characterization of weak mixing is in terms of absolute Cesàro averages: a probability preserving flow (X,ϕt,μ)(X,\phi_{t},\mu) is weakly mixing if and only if

limR→∞1R​∫0R|⟨f∘ϕt,g⟩|2​𝑑t→0,for all​f∈L02​(X),g∈L2​(X).\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{1}{R}\int_{0}^{R}\left|\langle f\circ\phi_{t},g\rangle\right|^{2}dt\to 0,\ \ \mbox{for all}\ f\in L^{2}_{0}(X),\ g\in L^{2}(X).

The flow is said to have the property of QWM with a rate hh for some increasing function h:[0,+∞)→[0,+∞)h:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty), h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0, if for all f∈L02​(X)f\in L^{2}_{0}(X) sufficiently “nice” and g∈L2​(X)g\in L^{2}(X),

(1.1) 1R​∫0R|⟨f∘ϕt,g⟩|2​𝑑t≤Cf,g⋅h⁡(R−1),\frac{1}{R}\int_{0}^{R}\left|\langle f\circ\phi_{t},g\rangle\right|^{2}dt\leq C_{f,g}\cdot h(R^{-1}),

see [25]. If this holds with h⁡(r)=rγh(r)=r^{\gamma}, we say that QWM holds with a Hölder rate γ\gamma, for h⁡(r)=(log⁡(1/r))−γh(r)=(\log(1/r))^{-\gamma} we say it is log\log-Hölder, etc.

Remark 1.1.

It is known that spectral bounds of the form

(1.2) σf​(Br​(ω))≤Cf​h​(r),ω∈ℝ,r∈(0,r0),∫f​𝑑μ=0,\sigma_{f}(B_{r}(\omega))\leq C_{f}h(r),\ \ \omega\in{\mathbb{R}},\ r\in(0,r_{0}),\ \ \int f\,d\mu=0,

imply QWM with the same rate, for the same ff. (It is essential that (1.2) be uniform in the spectral parameter ω\omega.) This was shown by Strichartz [34] for h⁡(r)=rαh(r)=r^{\alpha}, and extended by Last [26]; see Knill [25]. In the reverse direction, it was verified in [26, 25] that QWM with the rate h2h^{2} implies (1.2).

Let us return to the primitive substitution ζ\zeta. The Perron-Frobenius (PF) eigenvalue of 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta}, which we denote by α\alpha, plays an important role. Assume, for simplicity, that 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} is irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. If α\alpha is a Pisot number, which means that all the other eigenvalues of 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} are inside the open unit disk, then the substitution ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action and suspension flows over it have a large discrete component, hence not weakly mixing, see [13] (conjecturally, they are pure discrete, see [2]). The case when the second-largest eigenvalue satisfies |α2|>1|\alpha_{2}|>1 was studied in [5, 7]: under this assumption, QWM with a Hölder rate was obtained for Lebesgue almost every suspension vector s→\vec{s}. (There it was assumed that the test function is a “cylindrical function of level zero,” see the next section for definitions, which is, in a sense, the “nicest” function possible. In fact, this can be upgraded to the case of “weakly Lipschitz” test functions, see [9].) In [6] and [8] analogous results were obtained for almost every translation flow on a flat surface of genus 2. Forni [20], using a different method, obtained Hölder QWM for translation flows for an arbitrary genus ≥2\geq 2. After seeing his preprint, Bufetov and the second-named author obtained in [9] similar results, using a “symbolic approach”. More recently, Avila, Forni, and Safaee [3] established Hölder QWM for almost all interval exchange transformations (IET’s) of non-rotation type. Significantly, all of these results on QWM rely on the second Lyapunov exponent being positive, either for the Kontsevich-Zorich, or for the Rauzy-Zorich cocycle — the property which corresponds to |α2|>1|\alpha_{2}|>1 in the substitution case.

There are some isolated results which do not fall into the above scheme: Moll [28] obtained power-log QWM for a substitution conjugate to the Chacon map, for which 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} has an eigenvalue 1; in the IET setting this is related to another result in [3], namely, power-log QWM for almost all rotation class IET’s that are not rotations.

In this paper we obtain first quantitative estimates for suspension flows over Salem type substitutions, that is, when α\alpha is a Salem number. Recall that this means α\alpha is an algebraic integer, whose conjugates satisfy |αj|≤1|\alpha_{j}|\leq 1, with at least one of them on the unit circle. This is a “borderline” case, interesting from several points of view and generally more difficult to analyze. Our main result, which we state precisely in the next section, asserts that for Lebesgue a.e. suspension flow over a Salem type substitution, holds QWM with a rate that is a power of log⁡log\log\log, up to a log⁡log⁡log\log\log\log correction, namely, with a function

(1.3) hβ​(r):=exp⁡(−β​log⁡log​logα⁡(1/2​r)log⁡log⁡log​logα⁡(1/2​r)).h_{\beta}(r):=\exp\left(-\frac{\beta\log\log\log_{\alpha}(1/2r)}{\log\log\log\log_{\alpha}(1/2r)}\right).

Here “log\log” denotes the logarithm to base 2. On the other hand, we show that for any suspension vector s→\vec{s}, the resulting ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-action cannot have Hölder QWM.

As a rule, it is much harder to obtain results for a particular system than for a “typical” or “generic” one. In the case of a specific substitution with |α2|>1|\alpha_{2}|>1 it was shown in [5] that QWM holds with a log-Hölder rate for the self-similar suspension flow. Recently, analogous results were obtained for the substitution ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-action, see [10]. For Salem type substitutions, we are not aware of any QWM results in the literature. Considering the self-similar suspension flow over a Salem substitution, the first-named author obtained in [27] Hölder spectral bounds of the form (1.2), with h⁡(r)=rγ⁡(ω)h(r)=r^{\gamma(\omega)}, but only for algebraic spectral parameters ω∈ℚ⁡(α)\omega\in{\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) and with r0=r0​(ω)r_{0}=r_{0}(\omega). This was extended to the case of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-actions in [10] as well. These bounds are, unfortunately, not strong enough to yield any QWM rate. It turns out that a very weak, log∗\log^{*} QWM rate for the self-similar suspension flow may be deduced essentially by the same method as in [5]. Although we do not expect it to be sharp by any means, arguably, any quantitative rate is better than no rate. We sketch the derivation of this result in the Appendix.

A connection between spectral bounds for substitution flows and the decay rate of the Fourier transform for Bernoulli convolution measures (a much-studied class of self-similar “fractal” measures on the line, see [29, 35]), was pointed out in [5]. In the Appendix we recall this connection and note that the proof of QWM with a log∗\log^{*} rate also yields log∗\log^{*} Fourier decay for Salem Bernoulli convolutions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In the next section we present the background in more detail and state our main result. In Section 3 we prove the main theorem, and in Section 4 we show the absence of uniform Hölder bounds. We conclude in the Appendix as mentioned above.

2. Background and statement of results

2.3. Spectral theory: substitution flows

A useful general bound for twisted Birkhoff integrals in the context of substitution ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-actions was obtained in [5, Prop. 4.4] and [7, Prop. 3.2(ii)]. In order to state it, we need to introduce another definition.

A word v∈𝒜+v\in{\mathcal{A}}^{+} is called a return word for ζ\zeta if vv starts with a letter cc for some c∈𝒜c\in{\mathcal{A}} and v​cvc is admissible for the language of XζX_{\zeta}. From the uniform recurrence of (Xζ,T)(X_{\zeta},T) it follows that the set of irreducible return words (i.e., those which cannot be split into a concatenation of shorter return word) is finite and non-empty. A word vv is called a good return word for the substitution ζ\zeta if vv starts with some letter c∈𝒜c\in{\mathcal{A}} and v​cvc occurs as a subword in ζ⁡(b)\zeta(b) for every b∈𝒜b\in{\mathcal{A}}. Denote the set of good return words by G​R​(ζ)GR(\zeta). Denote by ℓ⁡(v)=[ℓ​(v)j]j≤d\ell(v)=[\ell(v)_{j}]_{j\leq d} the population vector of v∈𝒜+v\in{\mathcal{A}}^{+}, where ℓ​(v)j\ell(v)_{j} is the number of letters jj in vv.

Proposition 2.2 ([7, Prop. 3.2(ii)]).

for all R>1R>1, (x,t)∈Xζs→(x,t)\in{X^{\vec{s}}_{\zeta}}, and ω∈ℝ\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}.

(In [7, Prop. 3.2(ii)] the product is up to ⌊logα⁡R⌋−C2\lfloor\log_{\alpha}R\rfloor-C_{2}, for some C2>0C_{2}>0 depending on ζ\zeta, but this can be “absorbed” into C1C_{1} since λ<1\lambda<1 and ‖z‖≤12\|z\|\leq\frac{1}{2} for all z∈ℝz\in{\mathbb{R}}.)

Consider the Abelian group Γ\Gamma (a subgroup of OPENℤd){\mathbb{Z}}^{d}) generated by the population vectors of all return words for XζX_{\zeta}. We have 𝖲ζ​Γ⊂Γ{\sf S}_{\zeta}\Gamma\subset\Gamma, hence the real span of Γ\Gamma is a rational 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta}-invariant subspace. By assumption, 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} is irreducible, hence Γ\Gamma has full rank, i.e., it is a lattice. Passing to a sufficiently high power of the substitution, which does not change the substitution space, we can assume that every “elementary” return word (i.e., not a concatenation of shorter return words) is a good return word, and we obtain from Proposition 2.2, combined with [10, Lemma 4.2]:

2.4. Statement of results

Let ζ\zeta be a substitution of Salem type, i.e., the PF eigenvalue of the substitution matrix 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} is a Salem number and 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta} is irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. Our main result is as follows.

Theorem 2.3.

There exists β=β⁡(ζ)>0\beta=\beta(\zeta)>0 such that for Lebesgue-a.e. s→∈ℝ+d\vec{s}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+}, for every Lip-cylindrical function ff of mean zero, the spectral measure σf\sigma_{f} of the suspension flow (Xζs→,ϕt,μ~s→)({X^{\vec{s}}_{\zeta}},\phi_{t},\widetilde{\mu}_{\vec{s}}) satisfies

(2.4) σf(Br(ω))≤C~ζ,s→∥f∥∞2⋅hβ(r),r>0,wherehβ(r)=exp(−β​log⁡log​logα⁡(1/2​r)log⁡log⁡log​logα⁡(1/2​r)),\sigma_{f}(B_{r}(\omega))\leq\widetilde{C}_{\zeta,\vec{s}}\|f\|^{2}_{\infty}\cdot h_{\beta}(r),\ \ r>0,\ \ \ \mbox{where}\ \ h_{\beta}(r)=\exp\left(-\frac{\beta\log\log\log_{\alpha}(1/2r)}{\log\log\log\log_{\alpha}(1/2r)}\right),

for all ω∈ℝ\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}. Thus the system has QWM with the rate hβ​(r)h_{\beta}(r) for such functions ff.

We do not know if this is sharp; QWM with a log-Hölder rate seems more plausible. In any case, we know that Hölder QWM rate is impossible for any s→\vec{s}, see the next theorem. The idea of the proof of Theorem 2.3 is based on a variant of the Erdős-Kahane technique, in the framework of “vector expansions in base 𝖲ζ{\sf S}_{\zeta}”, developed in [10]. As in many other recent papers on QWM, the proof proceeds via (2.3), followed by Lemma 2.1. Thus we need to consider the distance from (𝖲ζ𝖳)n​ω​s→({\sf S}_{\zeta}^{\sf T})^{n}\omega\vec{s} to the nearest point in the lattice Γ∗\Gamma^{*}. We “win”, so to say, if this distance is not too small some of the time, in a quantitative way, which has to be uniform in the spectral parameter ω\omega. However, we do have some freedom in the choice of the roof vector s→\vec{s}, since we are allowed to throw away a set of measure zero.

Theorem 2.4.

For any substitution ζ\zeta of Salem type on dd symbols, for any s→∈ℝd\vec{s}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and any α>0\alpha>0, for almost every Lip-cylindrical function ff of mean zero, for any CfC_{f}, the inequality (1.2) is violated for h⁡(r)=rαh(r)=r^{\alpha}, for a sequence of R=Rn→∞R=R_{n}\to\infty.

The proof of Theorem 2.4 is analogous to the proof of [10, Theorem 2.7], which deals with the cases when s→=1→\vec{s}=\vec{1} and when s→\vec{s} is the PF eigenvector.

3. Proof of the Theorem 2.3

3.1. The set-up

By assumption, we have a substitution ζ\zeta on dd symbols with an irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} substitution matrix 𝖲ζ{\sf S_{\zeta}} having a Salem number α\alpha as the PF eigenvalue. The other eigenvalues are the Galois conjugates of α=α1\alpha=\alpha_{1}: they are α2=α−1\alpha_{2}=\alpha^{-1}, and the rest are α3,…,αd\alpha_{3},\ldots,\alpha_{d}, complex conjugate pairs of modulus one. Fix a height vector s→\vec{s} and thus the corresponding suspension flow (Xζs→,ϕt,μ~s→)({X^{\vec{s}}_{\zeta}},\phi_{t},\widetilde{\mu}_{\vec{s}}). Let A=𝖲ζ𝖳A={\sf S_{\zeta}^{T}} and we consider its action on ℂd{\mathbb{C}}^{d}. The matrix AA is diagonalizable over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}; we are going to use the decomposition of (real) vectors in terms of the (complex) basis of eigenvectors of AA. 4. Proof of lower bounds (no Hölder QWM for any suspension flow)

4.1. Some algebraic number theory (see e.g. [11])

. A number field is a finite field extension KK of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, and the degree of KK is the dimension of KK as a vector space over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}. An element α∈K\alpha\in K is an algebraic integer if it is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. Algebraic integers in KK form a ring denoted by 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K}.

Let K1,K2K_{1},K_{2} be two number fields. A ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-homomorphism between K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} is a field homomorphism σ:K1⟶K2\sigma:K_{1}\longrightarrow K_{2} such that σ⁡(r)=r\sigma(r)=r, for every r∈ℚr\in{\mathbb{Q}}. It is well known that there exist exactly dd distinct ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-homomorphisms between a number field KK of degree dd and ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. We will call these ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-homomorphisms between KK and ℂ{\mathbb{C}} the embeddings of KK into ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. If the image σ⁡(K)\sigma(K) is contained in ℝ{\mathbb{R}}, we will say σ\sigma is a real embedding. Note that if σ\sigma is not real, then σ¯\overline{\sigma} is another embedding, and we will call {σ,σ¯}\{\sigma,\overline{\sigma}\} a conjugate pair.

Let α1\alpha_{1} be an algebraic number and α2,…,αd\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{d} the rest of the roots of its minimal polynomial. In the particular case that K=ℚ⁡(α1)K={\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha_{1}), the dd distinct embeddings are completely determined by σj​(α1)=αj\sigma_{j}(\alpha_{1})=\alpha_{j}, j=1,…,dj=1,\dots,d. For η∈K\eta\in K, we call σ1​(η),…,σd​(η)\sigma_{1}(\eta),\dots,\sigma_{d}(\eta) the conjugates of η\eta. We define the trace of η∈K\eta\in K by Tr​(η)=∑σσ⁡(η)\textup{Tr}(\eta)=\sum_{\sigma}\sigma(\eta), where the sum runs over all embedding of KK in ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. In particular, if η∈𝒪K\eta\in\mathcal{O}_{K} then Tr​(η)∈ℤ\textup{Tr}(\eta)\in{\mathbb{Z}}.

4.2. Proof of Theorem 2.4

This is a minor variation of the proof of [10, Theorem 2.7], for which we need a version of [10, Lemma 6.2]. Thus we introduce notation consistent with [10] rather than with the earlier sections here.

Let A∈G​L​(d,ℤ)A\in GL(d,{\mathbb{Z}}) be an integer matrix, irreducible over ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, whose characteristic polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a Salem number α\alpha of degree d=2​m+2d=2m+2. Denote by α0=α−1\alpha_{0}=\alpha^{-1}, α1,α2​…​αm\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\dots\alpha_{m}, the real and complex conjugates of α\alpha in the (closed) upper half-plane, and let σ0,σ1,σ2,…,σm\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\dots,\sigma_{m} be the corresponding embeddings.

Let {ei}i=1d\{e_{i}\}^{d}_{i=1} be an eigenbasis of AA with entries in ℤ​[α]d{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha]^{d}. Consider a non-zero vector s→∈ℝd\vec{s}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} such that

s→=e1+C2​e2+⋯+Cd​ed,\vec{s}=e_{1}+C_{2}e_{2}+\dots+C_{d}e_{d},

that is, C1=1C_{1}=1. It is sufficient to consider such roof vectors for the suspension flow, since multiplying s→\vec{s} by a (positive) constant results in a measurably isomorphic ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-action.

For every ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 there exists η∈ℤ⁡[α]\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha] such that

The argument is very similar to that of [10, Lemma 6.2]. Denote ωv=ω⁡⟨e1,v⟩\omega^{v}=\omega\langle e_{1},v\rangle, for v∈ℤdv\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}. Then,

⟨ω​An​s→,v⟩\displaystyle\langle\omega A^{n}\vec{s},v\rangle =Tr⁡(ωv​αn)−σ0​(ωv)​α−n−∑j=1m(σj​(ωv)​αjn+σj​(ωv)¯​αj−n)\displaystyle={\rm Tr}(\omega^{v}\alpha^{n})-\sigma_{0}(\omega^{v})\alpha^{-n}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigl(\sigma_{j}(\omega^{v})\alpha^{n}_{j}+\overline{\sigma_{j}(\omega^{v})}\alpha^{-n}_{j}\bigr)
+C2​ωv​α−n+ωv​∑j=1m(C2​j+1​αjn+C2​j+1¯​αj−n)\displaystyle\quad+C_{2}\omega^{v}\alpha^{-n}+\omega^{v}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigl(C_{2j+1}\alpha^{n}_{j}+\overline{C_{2j+1}}\alpha^{-n}_{j}\bigr)
(4.2) =Tr⁡(ωv​αn)+(C2​ωv−σ0​(ωv))​α−n+∑j=1m(Hj​αjn+Hj¯​αj−n),\displaystyle={\rm Tr}(\omega^{v}\alpha^{n})+(C_{2}\omega^{v}-\sigma_{0}(\omega^{v}))\alpha^{-n}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigl(H_{j}\alpha_{j}^{n}+\overline{H_{j}}\alpha_{j}^{-n}\bigr),

where Hj=C2​j+1​ωv−σj​(ωv)H_{j}=C_{2j+1}\omega^{v}-\sigma_{j}(\omega^{v}). Consider the following embedding of ℚ⁡(α){\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) into ℝ2⊕ℂm≃ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\oplus{\mathbb{C}}^{m}\simeq{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (we identify ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with ℝ⊕ℝ{\mathbb{R}}\oplus{\mathbb{R}}):

τ:ω\displaystyle\tau:\omega ↦(ω,C2​ω−σ0​(ω),C3​ω−σ1​(ω),C5​ω−σ2​(ω),…,C2​m+1​ω−σm​(ω))\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\omega,&C_{2}\omega-\sigma_{0}(\omega),&C_{3}\omega-\sigma_{1}(\omega),&C_{5}\omega-\sigma_{2}(\omega),&\dots,&C_{2m+1}\omega-\sigma_{m}(\omega)\end{pmatrix}
≃(ω,C2​ω−σ0​(ω),Re⁡(C3​ω−σ1​(ω)),Im⁡(ω−σ1​(ω)),…,Im⁡(C2​m+1​ω−σm​(ω)))\displaystyle\simeq\begin{pmatrix}\omega,&C_{2}\omega-\sigma_{0}(\omega),&{\rm Re}(C_{3}\omega-\sigma_{1}(\omega)),&{\rm Im}(\omega-\sigma_{1}(\omega)),&\dots,&{\rm Im}(C_{2m+1}\omega-\sigma_{m}(\omega))\end{pmatrix}

The image of ℤ⁡[α]{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha] under this map is a lattice in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. Indeed, we just need to verify that for a basis of ℤ⁡[α]{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha], its image is a basis for ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. We may use the power basis given by {1,α,…,αd−1}\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{d-1}\}. It suffices to show that the determinant of the next square real matrix of dimension dd is different from zero:

M=(1C2−1Re⁡(C3−1)Im⁡(C3−1)⋯Im⁡(C2​m+1−1)αC2​α−α−1Re⁡(C3​α−α1)Im⁡(C3​α−α1)⋯Im⁡(C2​m+1​α−αm)αd−1C2​αd−1−α1−dRe⁡(C3​αd−1−α1d−1)Im⁡(C3​αd−1−α1d−1)⋯Im⁡(C2​m+1​αd−1−αmd−1))\footnotesize{M=\begin{pmatrix}1&C_{2}-1&{\rm Re}(C_{3}-1)&{\rm Im}(C_{3}-1)&\cdots&{\rm Im}(C_{2m+1}-1)\\ \alpha&C_{2}\alpha-\alpha^{-1}&{\rm Re}(C_{3}\alpha-\alpha_{1})&{\rm Im}(C_{3}\alpha-\alpha_{1})&\cdots&{\rm Im}(C_{2m+1}\alpha-\alpha_{m})\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ \alpha^{d-1}&C_{2}\alpha^{d-1}-\alpha^{1-d}&{\rm Re}(C_{3}\alpha^{d-1}-\alpha_{1}^{d-1})&{\rm Im}(C_{3}\alpha^{d-1}-\alpha_{1}^{d-1})&\cdots&{\rm Im}(C_{2m+1}\alpha^{d-1}-\alpha_{m}^{d-1})\end{pmatrix}}

(this is just the matrix (τ⁡(1),τ⁡(α),…,τ⁡(αd−1))𝖳(\tau(1),\tau(\alpha),\dots,\tau(\alpha^{d-1}))^{\sf T}) written explicitly). By elementary operations on the columns, which we can perform as vectors in ℂd{\mathbb{C}}^{d}, since it does not affect whether the determinant vanishes or not, we obtain the complex matrix

M~=(1111⋯1αα−1α3α4⋯αdαd−1α1−dα1d−1α1¯d−1⋯αm¯d−1),\widetilde{M}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1&1&\cdots&1\\ \alpha&\alpha^{-1}&\alpha_{3}&\alpha_{4}&\cdots&\alpha_{d}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ \alpha^{d-1}&\alpha^{1-d}&\alpha_{1}^{d-1}&\overline{\alpha_{1}}^{d-1}&\cdots&\overline{\alpha_{m}}^{d-1}\end{pmatrix},

whose determinant is not equal to zero, since it is the Vandermonde matrix of different numbers.

|∑i=0d−1niαi|<E,|∑i=0d−1niτj(αi)|<ε, for j=0,1,…,m.\left|\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}n_{i}\alpha^{i}\right|<E,\quad\left|\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}n_{i}\tau_{j}(\alpha^{i})\right|<{\varepsilon},\quad\text{ for }j=0,1,\dots,m.

The rest of the proof of Theorem 2.4 proceeds exactly as in [10, Section 6], the only difference being that the vector 𝟏{\bf 1} is replaced by a general vector s→\vec{s}. It is based on an upper bound for the lower local dimension of the spectral measure for a typical Lip-cylindrical function ff, which uses [10, Lemma 6.3], and [8, Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4], yielding that for any ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 and η=η⁡(ε)\eta=\eta({\varepsilon}) from Proposition 4.1 holds

precluding Hölder QWM. The reader is referred to [10] for details. ∎

Appendix B On the Fourier decay for Salem Bernoulli convolutions

B.1. Upper bound

For λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) and p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) let νλp\nu_{\lambda}^{p} be the distribution of the random series ∑n=0∞±λn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\pm\lambda^{n}, where the signs are chosen i.i.d., with probabilities p,1−pp,1-p. The “classical” Bernoulli convolutions are obtained for p=12p=\frac{1}{2}; the case when p≠12p\neq\frac{1}{2} is called “biased”. This is a remarkable family of “fractal” measures, which have been extensively studied for almost 100 years, but many open questions remain. It is not our intention to give a general survey of the topic; the reader is referred to [29, 35] and references therein. However, we do recall the principal results on Fourier decay. It is easily seen that

(B.1) ν^λp​(ξ)=∏n=0∞(p​e−2​π​i​λn​ξ+(1−p)​e2​π​i​λn​ξ),ν^λ1/2​(ξ)=∏n=0∞cos⁡(2​π​λn​ξ).\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)=\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}\Bigl(pe^{-2\pi i\lambda^{n}\xi}+(1-p)e^{2\pi i\lambda^{n}\xi}\Bigr),\ \ \ \ \ \widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{1/2}(\xi)=\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}\cos(2\pi\lambda^{n}\xi).

Erdős [17] discovered that if λ−1≠12\lambda^{-1}\neq\frac{1}{2} is a Pisot number, then ν^λp​(ξ)\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi) does not vanish at infinity. Later, Salem [33] proved that in all other cases lim|ξ|→∞ν^λp​(ξ)=0\lim_{|\xi|\to\infty}\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)=0. However, the question of decay rate is much more subtle and is still far from being resolved. Erdős [18] demonstrated that a power Fourier decay holds for Lebesgue-a.e. λ\lambda, and Kahane [23] showed that Erdős’ argument actually yields power Fourier decay for all λ\lambda outside of a set of Hausdorff dimension zero. Their argument forms a basis for what became known as the “Erdős-Kahane technique”. For specific λ\lambda our knowledge is rather poor. Kershner [24] obtained a power of the logarithm upper bound for Bernoulli convolutions corresponding to rational λ≠1/q\lambda\neq 1/q. In [5] such bounds were shown for non-Pisot and non-Salem algebraic integers. For other results on Fourier decay of self-similar measures, see [36, 32] and references therein. To our knowledge, in the literature there are no quantitative upper bounds for the Fourier decay of Salem Bernoulli convolutions, i.e., when λ=α−1\lambda=\alpha^{-1} is a reciprocal of a Salem number. We show that (admittedly, “super-weak”) log∗\log^{*} upper bound follows from Proposition A.3.

Corollary B.1.

Let α\alpha be a Salem number and λ=α−1\lambda=\alpha^{-1}. For p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) consider the biased Bernoulli convolution νλp\nu_{\lambda}^{p}. Then there exist A=Aα,pA=A_{\alpha,p} and C=Cα,pC=C_{\alpha,p}, such that

(B.2) |ν^λp​(ξ)|≤A​exp⁡(−C​log∗​|ξ|),|ξ|≥1.|\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)|\leq A\exp\bigl(-C\log^{*}|\xi|\bigr),\ \ |\xi|\geq 1.
Sketch of the proof.

We recall the (standard) proof of [5, Corollary A.3]. Let ξ∈[αN−1,αN]\xi\in[\alpha^{N-1},\alpha^{N}], and set t=α−N​ξt=\alpha^{-N}\xi. Then

|ν^λp(ξ)|=∏n=0∞|pe−2​π​i​λn​ξ+(1−p)e2​π​i​λn​ξ|≤∏n=0N−1|p+(1−p)e4​π​i​αn​t|≤∏n=0N−1(1−1−p2∥2αnt∥ℝ/ℤ2),\displaystyle|\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)|=\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}\Bigl|pe^{-2\pi i\lambda^{n}\xi}+(1-p)e^{2\pi i\lambda^{n}\xi}\Bigr|\leq\prod_{n=0}^{N-1}\Bigl|p+(1-p)e^{4\pi i\alpha^{n}t}\Bigr|\leq\prod_{n=0}^{N-1}\Bigl(1-{\frac{1-p}{2}}\|2\alpha^{n}t\|_{{}_{{\mathbb{R}}/{\mathbb{Z}}}}^{2}\Bigr),

using an elementary inequality |1+e2​π​i​τ|≤2−12∥τ∥ℝ/ℤ2|1+e^{2\pi i\tau}|\leq 2-\frac{1}{2}\|\tau\|_{{}_{{\mathbb{R}}/{\mathbb{Z}}}}^{2} for τ∈ℝ\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}. Now Proposition A.3 easily implies the desired claim. ∎

B.2. Lower bounds

For completeness, we briefly discuss lower bounds for |ν^λp​(ξ)||\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)|. They were suggested to us (in general terms, without details) by Peter Varjú [personal communication]. These bounds are based on an observation of Kahane [23] (see [29, Section 5] for a detailed exposition) that Salem Bernoulli convolutions can never have a power Fourier decay. They follow from the well-known result that for a Salem number α\alpha and ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 there exists a nonzero η∈ℤ⁡[α]\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}[\alpha], such that ‖η​αn‖ℝ/ℤ<ε\|\eta\alpha^{n}\|_{{\mathbb{R}}/{\mathbb{Z}}}<{\varepsilon} for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} (of which Proposition 4.1 is a generalization), with a quantitative bound similar to (4.3). We omit the details.

Proposition B.2.

Let α\alpha be a Salem number of degree dd, p∈(0,12)p\in(0,\frac{1}{2}), and suppose that γ>0\gamma>0 and C≥1C\geq 1 are such that for all ξ≥α\xi\geq\alpha holds

(B.3) |ν^λp​(ξ)|≤C​[logα⁡(ξ)]−γ,λ=α−1.\left|\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{p}(\xi)\right|\leq C[\log_{\alpha}(\xi)]^{-\gamma},\ \ \ \lambda=\alpha^{-1}.

Then

(B.4) γ≤12​(d−1)​logα​[(1−2​p)−1].\gamma\leq{\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}}(d-1)\log_{\alpha}[(1-2p)^{-1}].

For the unbiased Bernoulli convolution νλ=νλ1/2\nu_{\lambda}=\nu_{\lambda}^{1/2} we got a weaker lower bound. The difference between these cases comes from the fact that the terms of the product in (B.1) are bounded in absolute value from below by 1−2​p>01-2p>0, when p∈(0,12)p\in(0,\frac{1}{2}), whereas those for ν^λ1/2\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{1/2} vanish at αn/4\alpha^{n}/4 and 3​αn/43\alpha^{n}/4.

Proposition B.3.

Let α\alpha be a Salem number of degree dd, and suppose that β,γ>0\beta,\gamma>0 and C≥1C\geq 1 are such that for all ξ\xi sufficiently large holds

(B.5) |ν^λ1/2​(ξ)|≤C​[logα⁡(ξ)]−γ​(logα⁡logα⁡(ξ))β,λ=α−1.\left|\widehat{\nu}_{\lambda}^{1/2}(\xi)\right|\leq C[\log_{\alpha}(\xi)]^{-\gamma(\log_{\alpha}\log_{\alpha}(\xi))^{\beta}},\ \ \ \lambda=\alpha^{-1}.
